newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-MoDo result echoes forestry woes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-MoDo result echoes forestry woes.

text.p: Swedish forestry group Modo AB reported a sharp fall in 1996 profits on Wednesday, painting a similar dismal picture as its rivals in the gloomy sector where low prices are wiping out profits.
Despite currency hedging adding 1.45 billion crowns to its 1996 result, MoDo posted a profit after financial items of 2.92 billion crowns ($392 million) compared with 5.22 billion crowns in 1995.
Its shares were five crowns lower at 223 in afternoon trading after the news.
MoDo said the start of 1997 had shown good demand for fine paper and board products but there had been some weakening in the pulp market.
Analysts, who expected MoDo to post a profit of 3.06 billion crowns, said the result was in line with expectations.

"They had a one-off cost of 100 million crowns for redundancies and some pension costs for early retirement...but otherwise it was in line with expectations," said Claes Vikbladh, forestry analyst at Ohman.
"A large part of the profit in 1996 was due to currency hedging but everyone was aware of that."
Tumbling pulp and paper prices were behind the fall in profits, MoDo said, adding that newsprint prices had fallen further since the start of 1997.
It said demand remained strong in the fourth quarter of 1996 although a softening in demand for newsprint had been noted.
Stronger demand for fine paper which started in the summer continued in the fourth quarter and improved again at the start of 1997.
The company, suffering the fate of most forestry product companies in a sector in a cyclical downturn, was still able to lift its dividend to 9.00 crowns per share from 8.50.
"What they are saying is in line with the other forestry companies, that demand is good but they haven't been able to raise prices," Vikbladh said.
"The positive thing in the report is that they increased dividend. They are one of the few forestry companies in the world to increase dividend.
"That's a very positive sign. At least they believe that this is a profit level that could be sustained in the future."
Bjorn Danckwardt-Lilliestrom, forestry analyst at Handelsbanken, said the report contained no surprises.
"I think it was quite in line with expectations because they have taken one-time items of 100 million," he said.

"There was a lower result from currency hedging. I thought it would have been closer to 1.6 billion crowns and it turned out to be 1.5," he said. "There are absolutely no surprises on the market side."
MoDo was the third of Sweden's four large forestry companies to report its 1996 results.
Stora's 1996 profit plummeted to 2.35 billion crowns from 8.02 billion. The company blamed a weak economic trend in Europe in part for the collapse in profits.
Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget (SCA), Sweden's largest forestry company, reported profits fell 38 percent in 1996 to 3.57 billion crowns, hurt by lower prices and slack demand.
The fourth in the pack, AssiDoman, is to release its 1996 earnings on February 20. -- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700-1003 ($ = 7.448 Swedish Crowns)
